questions.question: Why does RIDGE apply a running median when estimating the noise PSD for whitening?

options.A: Its robust rejection of outliers prevents strong narrowband sinusoids from distorting the estimated noise floor
options.B: It resolves overlapping gravitational-wave polarizations without regularization
options.C: It estimates the distance to the trigger from the high-frequency PSD
options.D: It whitens only samples whose amplitude exceeds the Gaussian expectation

questions.rationale: The PSD example contains a strong sinusoidal outlier, and the running median is selected for outlier rejection in estimating the floor.
questions.evidence_quote: The main advantage of the running median is its ability to reject outliers.

questions.question: How are the whitening FIR coefficients obtained, and how is the resulting filter used?

options.A: They are estimated from a user-chosen training segment's PSD, then applied to a longer data stretch
options.B: They are estimated independently on every sample of the search segment and applied only backward in time
options.C: They are fitted to the simulated signal's hrss and reused as a line-removal filter
options.D: They are derived from the source sky-map and applied only to the detector with highest SNR

questions.rationale: The PSD from a user-specified training segment determines FIR coefficients used to whiten a longer stretch.
questions.evidence_quote: the filter coefficients are obtained using the PSD obtained from a user-specified training data segment.

questions.question: What vulnerability of training a whitening filter on an earlier segment do the authors identify?

options.A: Noise-floor nonstationarity on timescales shorter than the gap can make the trained filter inappropriate for later data
options.B: Any gap between training and search data mathematically destroys the FIR phase response
options.C: Training on more than two seconds forces the whitened variance above unity
options.D: A running-median PSD cannot be used when signals are present in the training segment

questions.rationale: The authors warn that a changing noise floor between separated segments can produce a mismatch in the needed whitening filter.
questions.evidence_quote: any non-stationarity in the noise ﬂoor on timescales shorter than the gap between the training and the processed data

questions.question: Why can MBLT remove line features without substantially damaging transient signals in the illustrated example?

options.A: Transient signals are outliers in the line-amplitude/phase time series and are rejected by its running-median estimate
options.B: The line-removal algorithm subtracts only frequencies above the transient's center frequency
options.C: The transient is reconstructed from the unwhitened PSD after the sinusoid is removed
options.D: The algorithm masks all times containing transients before estimating the line phase

questions.rationale: MBLT's running-median amplitude and phase estimates reject the transient outliers, leaving injected signals largely intact.
questions.evidence_quote: Transients signals appear as outliers in the amplitude/phase time series and are rejected by the running median estimate.

questions.question: What inverse problem motivates regularization in RIDGE's coherent network likelihood analysis?

options.A: Recovering two unknown polarization waveforms h+ and h× from a set of detector responses is ill-posed
options.B: Inferring the trigger's distance from one detector's calibrated strain is ill-posed
options.C: Estimating the instrument PSD from sky coordinates is underdetermined
options.D: Separating the co-located H1 and H2 antenna patterns requires an infinite gain

questions.rationale: Each detector measures a linear combination of the two polarizations, and prior work identifies inversion of these responses as ill-posed.
questions.evidence_quote: the problem of inverting a set of detector responses to obtain h+(t) and h×(t) is an ill-posed one

questions.question: How does the hard-constraint algorithm relate to the regularization scheme used for the reported results?

options.A: It is recovered in the limit of an infinitely large regulator gain factor
options.B: It is the zero-gain limit, where both polarizations are suppressed
options.C: It is identical only when the detector network has two instruments
options.D: It is obtained by averaging the regularized sky-map over all noise realizations

questions.rationale: The paper states that the hard constraint algorithm is the limiting case of the chosen regulator as its gain factor tends to infinity.
questions.evidence_quote: the hard constraint algorithm presented in [9] is actually obtained in the limit of an inﬁnitely large gain factor

questions.question: What distinguishes the less obvious detection statistic Rrad from simply using Rmm?

options.A: It measures radial displacement in a scaled plane of Rmm and peak likelihood relative to their no-signal ensemble means
options.B: It uses only the minimum likelihood over the sky and discards the ensemble baseline
options.C: It integrates detector strain coherently over frequency but ignores sky-map values
options.D: It is the ratio of peak likelihood to the known trigger distance

questions.rationale: Rrad combines normalized peak and max/min map quantities, referenced to the no-signal ensemble map S0.
questions.evidence_quote: The second statistic, Rrad, is the radial distance of the observed values

questions.question: What injection configuration was used to compare Rmm and Rrad in the Monte Carlo study?

options.A: Sine-Gaussian h+ and h× at 235 Hz and Q=9, in quadrature, from the GRB060813 sky position
options.B: A broadband chirp at 344 Hz with Q=2 from an isotropic sky distribution
options.C: A monochromatic 60 Hz signal with identical polarization phase from the Virgo location
options.D: A binary inspiral waveform at 16384 Hz centered on the detector zenith

questions.rationale: The injections were fixed at the real trigger location and used sine-Gaussian polarizations with a π/2 phase offset.
questions.evidence_quote: both sine-Gaussian signals having center frequency 235 Hz and a Q = 9.

questions.question: At what detection performance did the paper report for hrss=5×10−22 Hz−1/2, and what false-alarm interpretation accompanied it?

options.A: About 62% detection probability at false-alarm probability 10−2, corresponding to one false event per 50 seconds
options.B: About 50% detection probability at false-alarm probability 10−4, corresponding to one per 50 hours
options.C: About 62% detection probability at false-alarm rate 2×10−2 Hz, corresponding to one per 500 seconds
options.D: About 92% detection probability at false-alarm probability 10−2, corresponding to one per 5 seconds

questions.rationale: The results section gives ≃62% at 10−2 false alarm probability and explicitly interprets it as one event in 50 sec.
questions.evidence_quote: an hrss of 5 × 10−22 Hz−1/2 can be detected with ≃62% probability at a false alarm probability of 10−2.

questions.question: What limitation of the reported sensitivity estimates follows from the choice of 0.5-second integration segments?

options.A: They are lower bounds because segments greatly exceed the ∼40 ms injected signals; known FIR delays could later permit shorter integration
options.B: They are upper bounds because the data were downsampled below the signal bandwidth
options.C: They apply only to signals longer than 0.5 seconds, not burst signals
options.D: They cannot be compared across detectors because the FIR delays are unknown

questions.rationale: The authors state that 0.5 sec is much longer than the signals and chose it to accommodate filter delays; removing known delays should enable shorter segments.
questions.evidence_quote: This integration time is much larger than the ∼40 msec duration of the injected signals and, hence, the performance estimates we obtain here should be taken as lower bounds.
